alalal-e93935-d1e108.summary: Rubric of Article 9: whether faith, hope and charity are equal in the present life.

alalal-e93935-d1e115.summary: Introduces the question on Lombard's last chapter, which says that faith, hope, charity and works are equal.

alalal-e93935-d1e129.summary: Introduces objections that they are not equal.

alalal-e93935-d1e135.summary: First objection: we believe much more than we love, since there is nothing we do not believe, yet love falls short.

alalal-e93935-d1e144.summary: Second objection: in natural motions we do not always love what we know is lovable, so neither in spiritual ones need we love what we believe should be loved.

alalal-e93935-d1e160.summary: Third objection: saying this concerns the habits, infused together and contained in sanctifying grace, fails, since operation is not infused with them but follows them as an effect.

alalal-e93935-d1e178.summary: Fourth objection: Lombard's text says the equality concerns the intensity of interior acts, so the common reply that it concerns the spiritual quantity of habits fails.

alalal-e93935-d1e200.summary: Introduces arguments against denying the equality.

alalal-e93935-d1e207.summary: First: denial contradicts the saints, here and on Apocalypse 21:16, where the Gloss says the equal sides of the city are faith, hope, charity and works.

alalal-e93935-d1e221.summary: Second: when one virtue is infused all are, because of grace, of which each is a part; so when one grows all grow, and they are equal.

alalal-e93935-d1e237.summary: Third: if this equality applies to all virtues, why is it asserted here of these three?

alalal-e93935-d1e246.summary: Fourth: Gregory says charity, if present, works great things, and if it ceases to work it is not charity; so operation follows the quantity of charity.

alalal-e93935-d1e264.summary: Solution: equality is considered by habits, among the three virtues, and by acts, including the fourth, operation. Operation can be related to free choice, which exercises it, or to what informs and elicits it, grace. In the first respect operations of different virtues are not equal, nor does an act always match a virtue's full power, since one may love more or less fervently than one's charity. In the second respect they are equal, since a lesser operation informed by greater grace and charity merits eternal life more substantially than a greater one informed by lesser charity.
claims: Faith, hope and charity are equal as habits, and acts are equal in merit relative to the grace informing them.
The intensity of acts relative to free choice varies and need not match the virtue's power.
Merit depends on the grace and charity informing an act more than on the act's external magnitude.

alalal-e93935-d1e321.summary: Reply to the first: it concerns operation related to free choice, which varies with devotion and sadness since man never stays in one state, so acts differ; but relative to the grace eliciting and informing them, they are equal.

alalal-e93935-d1e343.summary: Reply to the second: natural affections are not united in one as the virtues are in grace; from that union it follows that when one grows all grow, and all are equal.

alalal-e93935-d1e360.summary: Reply to the third: Albert grants that it concerns not only the habits and that it applies to all virtues, but it is attributed specially to these because they alone are theological, tend immediately to God, and direct all others toward God, to whom all our work is referred.

alalal-e93935-d1e380.summary: Reply to Gregory: it concerns the act compared to the informing habit, not to free choice acting. Some reply that the equality is generic, each being great, not equal in amount; Albert rejects this, since the text expresses equality by 'as much as'.

alalal-e93935.summary: Article 9 examines Lombard's claim that faith, hope, charity and works are equal in this life. We seem to believe more than we love, and works follow habits rather than being infused with them. Yet the Gloss calls these the equal sides of the heavenly city, and the virtues grow together in grace. Albert distinguishes equality of habits, among the three virtues, from equality of acts, which includes works. Acts considered in relation to free choice vary with devotion and are not equal. Considered in relation to the grace and charity informing them they are equal, and a lesser act informed by greater charity merits more than a greater one with less. Natural affections lack this unity, which comes from the virtues' union in grace. The equality is ascribed especially to the theological virtues because they alone tend immediately to God and direct the others. Albert rejects reading the equality as merely generic, since the text speaks of equal amounts.
claims: Faith, hope and charity are equal as habits united in grace.
Acts are unequal in relation to free choice but equal in merit relative to the grace informing them.
Merit depends on the charity informing an act more than on its external magnitude.
The theological virtues alone tend immediately to God and direct all the other virtues.
